{{Short description|British physicist (1923–1996)}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=April 2022}}
'''Peter Howard Fowler''' [[Fellow of the Royal Society|FRS]] (27 February 1923&nbsp;— 8 November 1996) was a British physicist and academic.<ref name="obit Ind">{{cite news |last1=Perkins |first1=D. H. |author1-link=Donald Hill Perkins |title=Obituary: Professor Peter Fowler |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/obituaries/obituary-professor-peter-fowler-1352277.html |access-date=26 August 2024 |work=The Independent |date=14 November 1996}}</ref>

==Life==
Fowler was educated at [[Summer Fields School]], [[Winchester College]], and under [[Cecil Powell]] at the [[University of Bristol]].<ref name=RS>{{cite journal|last1=Wolfendale|first1=Arnold|title=Peter Howard Fowler. 27 February 1923-8 November 1996|journal=Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society|date=1998|volume=44|pages=176–189|jstor=770238|doi=10.1098/rsbm.1998.0012|doi-access=free}}</ref>

Fowler researched primary [[cosmic radiation]], measuring the presence of beryllium, boron, and lithium in [[cosmic rays]]. He developed improved methods for measuring cosmic rays, using high-altitude balloons and later jets, and investigated the radiation hazards of high-altitude supersonic flight. He studied radioactive fallout from the 1986 [[Chernobyl]] nuclear power station explosion in Ukraine, and after the 1988 Lockerbie aircraft bombing he developed a thermal neutron-based methodology for screening passengers' luggage.{{fact|date=July 2024}}

Fowler served as a [[radar]] officer in the wartime RAF (1942–46). Following the D-Day landings, RAF bombers soon experienced intensive German jamming of their [[Gee-H (navigation)|Gee navigation system]]. He used his skills to detect the interference signals and through analysis was able to locate the station responsible, which was subsequently destroyed. It is reported{{who|date=July 2024}} that Goering demanded a court martial over what the Axis powers viewed as a breach of security as they did not believe that it was possible to locate a jamming station so rapidly.<ref>{{cite news |title=Professor Peter Fowler |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-independent-obituary-for-peter-howar/200890187/|author=D. H. Perkins |work=The Independent |date=14 November 1996 |pages=16}}</ref>

==Awards==

Fowler won the 1974 [[Hughes Medal]] of the [[Royal Society]] "for his outstanding contributions to cosmic ray and elementary particle physics".<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.iupap.org/commissions/c4/cosnews/cosnews38.html|title=CosNews No. 28, Spring 1997|publisher=International Union of Pure and Applied Physics|access-date=2009-02-06|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081120044713/http://www.iupap.org/commissions/c4/cosnews/cosnews38.html|archive-date=2008-11-20}}</ref>

==Family==

Fowler was married in 1949 [[Bathavon Rural District|Bathavon, Somerset]] to the physicist [[Rosemary Fowler]] nee Brown.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-024-00109-5|title=Nature |date=15 January 2024}}</ref> Their daughter is [[Mary Fowler (geologist)|Mary Fowler]], former Master of [[Darwin College, Cambridge]]. His father was the physicist Sir [[Ralph Howard Fowler]], who determined the state of matter in [[white dwarf]] stars. His grandfather was [[Lord Ernest Rutherford]], who discovered the [[atomic nucleus]].
